answer.rationale: Finance's 18% cut target and a non-auto-renewing contract 14 days out make negotiation the only path that can deliver TCO reduction without changing the supplier footprint. Memory c4 shows that pressing the incumbent at renewal has historically moved both price and terms (high reliability), and c6 confirms multi-year terms with the incumbent unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. Memory c2 is worth verifying because, although it records a successful past low-cost vendor switch, the current situation has a 94% utilization line with no buffer; introducing an unverified primary vendor mid-cycle is exactly the kind of delivery-risk increase the primary objective forbids. Staying with the incumbent via negotiate_terms preserves the stable integration (c1) and the proven margin-recovery pattern (c4) while we capture the 18% through negotiation rather than migration. add_second_source is a future-cycle option (c3-style resilience) but does not, by itself, hit this year's 18% cost reduction in time. defer_decision (c5) is rejected because the contract does not auto-renew and lapsing would force an emergency renewal on unfavorable terms. switch_primary_vendor is rejected on delivery-risk grounds given the no-buffer, high-utilization line and would require onboarding during a 94% utilization window. The other available action, add_second_source, can be retained as a planned resilience step at next review if negotiation alone does not reach the 18% target.
